claim: More than 100 unique inbred mouse strains were examined for liver steatosis and related traits after being fed a diet rich in fat and carbohydrates.
source: To identify genetic and environmental factors contributing to the pathogenesis of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, we examined liver steatosis and related clinical and molecular traits in more than 100 unique inbred mouse strains, which were fed a diet rich in fat and carbohydrates.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of strains examined and the dietary intervention used.

claim: A greater than 30-fold variation in hepatic triglyceride accumulation was observed among the mouse strains.
source: A >30-fold variation in hepatic TG accumulation was observed among the strains.
evidence: The abstract reports the observed variation in hepatic TG accumulation across strains.

claim: Genome-wide association studies revealed three loci associated with hepatic triglyceride accumulation.
source: Genome-wide association studies revealed three loci associated with hepatic TG accumulation.
evidence: The abstract states the number of loci identified through GWAS.

claim: Gde1 is a high-confidence candidate gene for hepatic steatosis identified through transcriptomic data from liver and adipose tissue.
source: Utilizing transcriptomic data from the liver and adipose tissue, we identified several high-confidence candidate genes for hepatic steatosis, including Gde1, a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase not previously implicated in triglyceride metabolism.
evidence: The abstract identifies Gde1 as a candidate gene based on transcriptomic analysis.

claim: Gde1 had not been previously implicated in triglyceride metabolism.
source: Utilizing transcriptomic data from the liver and adipose tissue, we identified several high-confidence candidate genes for hepatic steatosis, including Gde1, a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase not previously implicated in triglyceride metabolism.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that Gde1 was not previously implicated in TG metabolism.

claim: The role of Gde1 in hepatic steatosis was confirmed by in vivo hepatic over-expression studies.
source: We confirmed the role of Gde1 by in vivo hepatic over-expression and shRNA knockdown studies.
evidence: The abstract states that overexpression studies confirmed Gde1's role.

claim: The role of Gde1 in hepatic steatosis was confirmed by shRNA knockdown studies.
source: We confirmed the role of Gde1 by in vivo hepatic over-expression and shRNA knockdown studies.
evidence: The abstract states that knockdown studies confirmed Gde1's role.

claim: Gde1 expression increases triglyceride production by contributing to the production of glycerol-3-phosphate.
source: We hypothesize that Gde1 expression increases TG production by contributing to the production of glycerol-3-phosphate.
evidence: The abstract presents a hypothesis about the mechanism by which Gde1 affects TG production.

claim: NAFLD encompasses a spectrum of liver abnormalities ranging from steatosis through NASH to fibrosis and cirrhosis in the absence of excessive alcohol consumption and hepatitis viral infection.
source: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) encompasses a wide spectrum of liver abnormalities, ranging from benign hepatocellular accumulation of lipids (steatosis), through non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), to fibrosis and cirrhosis in the absence of excessive consumption of alcohol and hepatitis viral infection.
evidence: The introduction defines NAFLD and its spectrum of manifestations.

claim: Advanced NAFLD can progress to end-stage liver disease with increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Advanced NAFLD can eventually progress to end-stage liver disease with increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (Kopec and Burns, 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites literature supporting the progression of NAFLD to HCC.

claim: NAFLD is strongly associated with obesity, diabetes, and dyslipidemia.
source: Population studies have shown that NAFLD is strongly associated with obesity, diabetes, and dyslipidemia (Marchesini et al., 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites population studies showing associations between NAFLD and metabolic conditions.

claim: NAFLD can be viewed as the hepatic manifestation of the metabolic syndrome.
source: As such, NAFLD can be viewed as the hepatic manifestation of the metabolic syndrome.
evidence: The introduction presents a conceptual framework for understanding NAFLD.

claim: NAFLD is rapidly becoming the most common form of chronic liver disease worldwide.
source: With the increasing prevalence of obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, it is not surprising that NAFLD is rapidly becoming the most common form of chronic liver disease worldwide (Ratziu et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on the increasing prevalence of NAFLD.

claim: It is estimated that 20-30% of the population in Western developed countries is affected by NAFLD.
source: It is estimated that 20–30% of the population in Western developed countries is affected (Vernon et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites an estimate of NAFLD prevalence in Western countries.

claim: Simple steatosis appears to be benign and non-progressive in the majority of individuals affected with NAFLD.
source: Although simple steatosis appears to be benign and non-progressive in the majority of individuals affected with NAFLD (Teli et al., 1995), excessive fat accumulation in the liver is associated with organ pathology, including NASH and cirrhosis.
evidence: The introduction cites literature on the natural history of simple steatosis.

claim: NASH frequently progresses to fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver failure, and hepatocellular carcinoma, resulting in poor long-term prognosis.
source: NASH frequently progresses to fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver failure, and HCC, resulting in poor long-term prognosis.
evidence: The introduction describes the progression and outcomes of NASH.

claim: Subtle genetic variations and environmental factors play a role in determining the disease phenotype and progression of NAFLD.
source: The factors determining the progressive phenotype of this complex disease remain largely unknown, although it is clear that subtle genetic variations and environmental factors (such as diet and lifestyle) play a role in determining the disease phenotype and progression (Day, 2002; Anstee et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites literature on genetic and environmental contributions to NAFLD.

claim: According to the 'two-hit hypothesis' model, the first insult involves lipid accumulation in hepatocytes due to an imbalance in triglyceride homeostasis.
source: According to the prevailing 'two-hit hypothesis' model (Day and James, 1998), it is believed that the first insult involves lipid accumulation in the hepatocytes, due to an imbalance in triglyceride homeostasis.
evidence: The introduction cites the two-hit hypothesis model for NAFLD pathogenesis.

claim: Steatosis increases the vulnerability of the liver to a 'second hit', which promotes liver injury, oxidative stress, inflammation, and fibrosis.
source: Subsequently, steatosis increases the vulnerability of the liver to a 'second hit', which promotes liver injury, oxidative stress, inflammation, and fibrosis.
evidence: The introduction describes the second hit in the two-hit hypothesis.

claim: Silencing of DGAT2 by an antisense oligo improved steatosis but worsened liver injury and fibrosis in mice.
source: However, silencing of diacylglycerol acyltransferase 2 (DGAT2) by an antisense oligo improved steatosis but worsened liver injury and fibrosis in mice (Yamaguchi et al., 2007).
evidence: The introduction cites a study showing paradoxical effects of DGAT2 silencing.

claim: DGAT2-knockdown mice exhibit increased fatty acid oxidation through CYP2E1, leading to increased oxidative stress, inflammation, and tissue damage.
source: DGAT2-knockdown mice exhibit increased fatty acid (FA) oxidation through CYP2E1, leading to increased oxidative stress, inflammation, and tissue damage.
evidence: The introduction describes the mechanism of liver injury in DGAT2-knockdown mice.

claim: Steatosis may be an adaptive response to protect the liver from lipotoxicity through partitioning toxic lipids into stable intracellular triglyceride stores.
source: These findings lead to the proposal that steatosis may be an adaptive response to protect the liver from lipotoxicity through partitioning toxic lipids into stable intracellular triglyceride stores.
evidence: The introduction presents a hypothesis about the protective role of steatosis.

claim: Triglyceride accumulation per se is not the 'first hit' but the underlying inability to compensate for increased fatty acid flux makes the liver prone to subsequent oxidative damage.
source: These data suggest that TG accumulation per se is not the 'first hit' but the underlying inability to compensate for increased FA flux, which makes the liver prone to subsequent oxidative damage.
evidence: The introduction presents an interpretation of the DGAT2 knockdown data.

claim: There exists no established therapy targeting NAFLD.
source: So far, there exists no established therapy targeting NAFLD.
evidence: The introduction states the current state of NAFLD treatment.

claim: Treatment options for NAFLD aim at weight reduction, control of dyslipidemia and improving insulin sensitivity through lifestyle changes and pharmacological agents.
source: Since most NAFLD patients suffer from obesity and insulin resistance, treatment options aim at weight reduction, control of dyslipidemia and improving insulin sensitivity through lifestyle changes and pharmacological agents, such as metformin, statins, fibrates, and thiazolidinediones (Schreuder et al., 2008).
evidence: The introduction cites current treatment approaches for NAFLD.

claim: In humans, 15% of hepatic triglyceride comes directly from the diet, 26% from de novo lipogenesis, and 59% from adipose tissue in the form of non-esterified fatty acids.
source: In humans, it is estimated that 15% of hepatic TG comes directly from the diet, 26% from de novo lipogenesis, and 59% from adipose tissue in the form of non-esterified FAs (Donnelly et al., 2005).
evidence: The introduction cites estimates of the sources of hepatic TG in humans.

claim: The adipose tissue and liver together supply more than 85% of fatty acids for the biosynthesis of triglyceride in the liver.
source: Together, the adipose tissue and liver play a major role in hepatic TG accumulation and supply >85% of FAs for the biosynthesis of TG in the liver.
evidence: The introduction summarizes the major sources of hepatic TG.

claim: Genetics plays a substantial role in determining the susceptibility to the development of NAFLD.
source: Epidemiologic studies in human populations and animal studies indicate that genetics plays a substantial role in determining the susceptibility to the development of NAFLD (Browning et al., 2004; Guerrero et al., 2009; Kahle et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites studies supporting a genetic contribution to NAFLD.

claim: The coexistence of NASH and cirrhosis clusters within families supports the existence of a common genetic link.
source: The coexistence of NASH and cirrhosis clusters within families supports the existence of a common genetic link (Struben et al., 2000; Willner et al., 2001).
evidence: The introduction cites familial clustering studies supporting genetic factors.

claim: The broad-sense heritability of hepatic steatosis has been estimated to be approximately 39% after adjustment for age, sex, race, and body mass index.
source: The broad-sense heritability of hepatic steatosis has been estimated to be ∼39% after adjustment for age, sex, race, and body mass index (Schwimmer et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites a heritability estimate for hepatic steatosis.

claim: Additional independent genetic factors beyond those predisposing to obesity and diabetes contribute to the susceptibility to NAFLD.
source: Although genetic predisposition to obesity and diabetes undoubtedly explains a fraction of the genetic component, additional independent genetic factors clearly contribute to the susceptibility to NAFLD (Browning et al., 2004).
evidence: The introduction cites evidence for NAFLD-specific genetic factors.

claim: Only a small fraction of genes accounting for fatty liver disease have been identified.
source: To date, only a small fraction of genes accounting for fatty liver disease have been identified and the molecular pathogenesis of NAFLD is poorly understood.
evidence: The introduction states the current state of knowledge about NAFLD genetics.

claim: The high-fat, high-sucrose diet has previously been shown to have a profound effect on obesity and insulin resistance depending upon the genetic background.
source: This diet has previously been shown to have a profound effect on obesity and insulin resistance depending upon the genetic background (Parks et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites previous work characterizing the diet used.

claim: Hepatic triglyceride content was significantly correlated with liver weight (r = 0.38, p = 5.75 × 10−14).
source: Hepatic TG content was significantly correlated with the liver weight (r = 0.38, p = 5.75 × 10−14, Figure 1B).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between hepatic TG and liver weight, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Less than threefold difference in cholesterol and phospholipid levels was observed among the strains.
source: Contrary to the large variations in TG among strains, less than threefold difference in cholesterol and phospholipid levels was observed among the strains (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section reports the variation in other lipid species.

claim: Triglyceride content in the liver was positively correlated with hepatic total cholesterol content (r = 0.35, p = 1.18 × 10−12).
source: The TG content in the liver was positively correlated with hepatic total cholesterol (TC) content (r = 0.35, p = 1.18 × 10−12, Figure 1C) but negatively correlated with the levels of phospholipids (r = −0.26, p = 3.45 × 10−7, Figure 1D).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between hepatic TG and other lipids, with reference to figures.

claim: Triglyceride content in the liver was negatively correlated with the levels of phospholipids (r = −0.26, p = 3.45 × 10−7).
source: The TG content in the liver was positively correlated with hepatic total cholesterol (TC) content (r = 0.35, p = 1.18 × 10−12, Figure 1C) but negatively correlated with the levels of phospholipids (r = −0.26, p = 3.45 × 10−7, Figure 1D).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between hepatic TG and phospholipids, with reference to figures.

claim: Increased neutral lipids content, in particular triglyceride, contributes significantly to enlarged livers.
source: These data suggest that increased neutral lipids content, in particular TG, contributes significantly to the enlarged livers.
evidence: The results section interprets the correlation data.

claim: A large variation in alanine aminotransferase activities was observed among the strains.
source: Similar to hepatic TG content, we also observed a large variation in ALT activities among the strains.
evidence: The results section reports variation in ALT activities.

claim: Plasma alanine aminotransferase activities showed a positive correlation with hepatic triglyceride levels.
source: Plasma ALT activities showed a positive correlation with hepatic TG levels, implicating a role of increased hepatic TG levels in liver damage (Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between ALT and hepatic TG, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Histologic examination of livers from a subset of strains including some with high triglyceride did not observe evidence of significant pathology other than lipid accumulation.
source: We performed histologic examination of livers from a subset of strains including some with high TG and did not observe evidence of significant pathology other than lipid accumulation (data not shown).
evidence: The results section reports histological findings.

claim: mRNA levels of markers for B-lymphocytes (CD45/PTPPRC) and macrophages (CD68) were not increased in steatotic liver samples.
source: Furthermore, mRNA levels of markers for B-lymphocytes (CD45/PTPPRC) and macrophages (CD68) were not increased in steatotic liver samples (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The results section reports gene expression data for immune cell markers, with reference to figures.

claim: Markers for T cells, B cells, and leukocytes were not increased in steatotic livers.
source: Similarly, markers for other immune cells, such as T cells (Cd28, Csf2, Cd4, Ccr5, Gata3 Cxcr4), B cells (Pax5, Cd70, Cd79b), and leukocytes (Cd33, Cd52, Cd53, Cd44, Prg2) were also not increased (data not shown), suggesting the absence of significant immune cell infiltration and steatohepatitis in these mice after 8 weeks on the HF/HS diet.
evidence: The results section reports gene expression data for additional immune cell markers.

claim: Hepatic triglyceride content was poorly correlated with plasma triglyceride levels (r = −0.13, p = 0.0115).
source: Hepatic TG content was poorly correlated with plasma TG levels (r = −0.13, p = 0.0115, Figure 3A), whereas it was positively correlated with plasma cholesterol levels (r = 0.41, p = 5.04 × 10−17, Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between hepatic TG and plasma lipids, with reference to figures.

claim: Hepatic triglyceride content was positively correlated with plasma cholesterol levels (r = 0.41, p = 5.04 × 10−17).
source: Hepatic TG content was poorly correlated with plasma TG levels (r = −0.13, p = 0.0115, Figure 3A), whereas it was positively correlated with plasma cholesterol levels (r = 0.41, p = 5.04 × 10−17, Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between hepatic TG and plasma cholesterol, with reference to figures.

claim: The correlation between hepatic triglyceride levels and plasma free fatty acids levels was not significant (r = 0.04, p = 0.44).
source: The correlation between hepatic TG levels and plasma free FAs (FFAs) levels was not significant (r = 0.04, p = 0.44); however, hepatic TG levels were correlated with plasma glycerol levels (r = 0.20, p = 0.0001, Figure 3C), suggesting a link between liver steatosis and lipolysis in the adipose tissue.
evidence: The results section reports the lack of correlation between hepatic TG and plasma FFAs.

claim: Hepatic triglyceride levels were correlated with plasma glycerol levels (r = 0.20, p = 0.0001).
source: The correlation between hepatic TG levels and plasma free FAs (FFAs) levels was not significant (r = 0.04, p = 0.44); however, hepatic TG levels were correlated with plasma glycerol levels (r = 0.20, p = 0.0001, Figure 3C), suggesting a link between liver steatosis and lipolysis in the adipose tissue.
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between hepatic TG and plasma glycerol, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: There was a robust association between hepatic steatosis and plasma insulin (r = 0.47, p = 4.51 × 10−21).
source: Similar to the findings in humans, there was a robust association between hepatic steatosis and plasma insulin (r = 0.47, p = 4.51 × 10−21, Figure 3D), glucose (r = 0.23, p = 1.26 × 10−5, Figure 3E) as well as insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) (r = 0.45, p = 2.18 × 10−20, Figure 3F).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between hepatic steatosis and metabolic parameters, with reference to figures.

claim: There was a robust association between hepatic steatosis and plasma glucose (r = 0.23, p = 1.26 × 10−5).
source: Similar to the findings in humans, there was a robust association between hepatic steatosis and plasma insulin (r = 0.47, p = 4.51 × 10−21, Figure 3D), glucose (r = 0.23, p = 1.26 × 10−5, Figure 3E) as well as insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) (r = 0.45, p = 2.18 × 10−20, Figure 3F).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between hepatic steatosis and glucose, with reference to figures.

claim: There was a robust association between hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) (r = 0.45, p = 2.18 × 10−20).
source: Similar to the findings in humans, there was a robust association between hepatic steatosis and plasma insulin (r = 0.47, p = 4.51 × 10−21, Figure 3D), glucose (r = 0.23, p = 1.26 × 10−5, Figure 3E) as well as insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) (r = 0.45, p = 2.18 × 10−20, Figure 3F).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between hepatic steatosis and HOMA-IR, with reference to figures.

claim: There was a robust correlation between hepatic triglyceride levels and adiposity (r = 0.59, p = 6.70 × 10−35).
source: Consistent with this finding, there was a robust correlation between hepatic TG levels and adiposity (r = 0.59, p = 6.70 × 10−35, Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between hepatic TG and adiposity, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Steatosis was associated with increased subcutaneous, gonadal and mesenteric fat mass but not with retroperitoneal fat content.
source: We dissected the individual fat depots and found that steatosis was associated with increased subcutaneous, gonadal and mesenteric fat mass but not with retroperitoneal fat content (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: The results section reports associations between steatosis and specific fat depots, with reference to figures.

claim: Cd36 had the highest correlation with triglyceride levels in the liver (r = 0.70, p = 1.85 × 10−17).
source: In the liver, Cd36 had the highest correlation with TG levels (r = 0.70, p = 1.85 × 10−17).
evidence: The results section reports the gene with the highest correlation to hepatic TG.

claim: CD36 is a multifunctional protein that enhances cellular fatty acid uptake.
source: CD36 is a multifunctional protein that enhances cellular FA uptake.
evidence: The results section describes the function of CD36.

claim: CD36-deficient mice are resistant to the induction of hepatic steatosis by alcohol and high-carbohydrate feeding.
source: Previous studies have shown that CD36-deficient mice are resistant to the induction of hepatic steatosis by alcohol and high-carbohydrate feeding (Clugston et al., 2014).
evidence: The results section cites previous work on CD36-deficient mice.

claim: Expression of the proto-oncogene c-Jun was positively correlated with hepatic triglyceride content (r = 0.51, p = 7.05 × 10−09).
source: Interestingly, expression of the proto-oncogene c-Jun was positively correlated with hepatic TG content (r = 0.51, p = 7.05 × 10−09).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between c-Jun expression and hepatic TG.

claim: Enhanced hepatic c-Jun levels were observed in NAFLD patients, which correlated with inflammation and the degree of hepatic steatosis.
source: Enhanced hepatic c-Jun levels were observed in NAFLD patients, which correlated with inflammation and the degree of hepatic steatosis (Dorn et al., 2014).
evidence: The results section cites literature on c-Jun in NAFLD patients.

claim: Increased c-Jun/AP-1 activation has been implicated in the progression of NAFLD.
source: Increased c-Jun/AP-1 activation has been implicated in the progression of NAFLD (Dorn et al., 2014; Hasenfuss et al., 2014).
evidence: The results section cites literature on c-Jun/AP-1 in NAFLD progression.

claim: Prkcb expression was significantly correlated with hepatic steatosis (r = 0.58, p = 1.62 × 10−11) in adipose tissue.
source: Prkcb (protein kinase cβ), whose expression was significantly correlated with hepatic steatosis (r = 0.58, p = 1.62 × 10−11), has been shown to be important in adipose tissue remodeling and FA metabolism (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between Prkcb expression in adipose and hepatic steatosis.

claim: Prkcb-null mice are protected against diet-induced obesity and the development of hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance.
source: Prkcb-null mice are protected against diet-induced obesity and the development of hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance (Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: The results section cites literature on Prkcb-null mice.

claim: Cd53 was highly correlated with hepatic steatosis (r = 0.58, p = 2.06 × 10−11) in adipose tissue.
source: Cd53, an adipose inflammatory marker, was also highly correlated with hepatic steatosis (r = 0.58, p = 2.06 × 10−11).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between Cd53 expression in adipose and hepatic steatosis.

claim: Cd53 was significantly up-regulated in preadipocytes from obese human subjects.
source: Previous microarray profiling showed that Cd53 was significantly up-regulated in preadipocytes from obese human subjects (Nair et al., 2005).
evidence: The results section cites literature on Cd53 expression in human obesity.

claim: Hcst was highly correlated with hepatic triglyceride content (r = 0.57, p = 9.64 × 10−11) in adipose tissue.
source: Hcst (hematopoietic cell signal transducer), previously shown to be a key hub gene in gene co-expression network that was significantly associated with serum TG levels (Haas et al., 2012) in humans, was also highly correlated with hepatic TG content (r = 0.57, p = 9.64 × 10−11).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between Hcst expression in adipose and hepatic TG.

claim: Hoxa5 expression was negatively correlated with hepatic triglyceride content (r = −0.56, p = 1.37 × 10−10) in adipose tissue.
source: In our study, Hoxa5 expression was negatively correlated with hepatic TG content (r = −0.56, p = 1.37 × 10−10).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between Hoxa5 expression in adipose and hepatic TG.

claim: Hoxa5 has previously been shown to be up-regulated after fat loss in human patients who have undergone bariatric surgery.
source: The homeobox transcription factor Hoxa5 has previously been shown to be up-regulated after fat loss in human patients who have undergone bariatric surgery (Dankel et al., 2010).
evidence: The results section cites literature on Hoxa5 expression after bariatric surgery.

claim: A missense mutation in LRRFIP1 was associated with adiposity and inflammation in human GWAS studies.
source: Human GWAS studies have shown that a missense mutation in LRRFIP1 was associated with adiposity and inflammation (Plourde et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section cites human GWAS findings for LRRFIP1.

claim: Lrrfip1 expression was significantly associated with hepatic steatosis (r = 0.56, p = 1.89 × 10−10) in adipose tissue.
source: Lrrfip1 expression was significantly associated with hepatic steatosis in our study (r = 0.56, p = 1.89 × 10−10).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between Lrrfip1 expression in adipose and hepatic steatosis.

claim: Adrb3 expression was negatively correlated with hepatic triglyceride levels (r = −0.56, p = 2.34 × 10−10) in adipose tissue.
source: In our study, Adrb3 expression was negatively correlated with hepatic TG levels (r = −0.56, p = 2.34 × 10−10).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between Adrb3 expression in adipose and hepatic TG.

claim: Adrb3 activation induces white adipose remodeling and brown adipogenesis.
source: Adrb3 (β3-adrenergic receptor) activation induces white adipose remodeling and brown adipogensis (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: The results section cites literature on Adrb3 function.

claim: Increased expression of Lipa was found to be associated with hepatic steatosis (r = 0.56, p = 2.63 × 10−10) in adipose tissue.
source: Increased expression of Lipa (lysosomal acid lipase), which is involved in lysosomal lipophagy and TG/cholesterol ester catabolism, was found to be associated with hepatic steatosis (r = 0.56, p = 2.63 × 10−10).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between Lipa expression in adipose and hepatic steatosis.

claim: Enrichment analysis using the top 1000 hepatic genes correlated with hepatic triglyceride levels showed a significant enrichment of mitochondrial genes (1.57 fold, adjusted p = 1.99 × 10−5).
source: Enrichment analysis using the top 1000 hepatic genes correlated with hepatic TG levels (Table 3) showed a significant enrichment of mitochondrial genes (1.57 fold, adjusted p = 1.99 × 10−5).
evidence: The results section reports pathway enrichment analysis results.

claim: Among the 127 mitochondrial genes, the majority (100 genes) were higher in steatotic livers.
source: Among the 127 mitochondrial genes, the majority (100 genes) were higher in steatotic livers, suggesting that altered mitochondria function is linked to the disease process of NAFLD.
evidence: The results section reports the direction of expression changes for mitochondrial genes.

claim: Components of the extracellular matrix were enriched (2.91 fold, adjusted p = 5.89 × 10−3) among the top 1000 hepatic genes correlated with hepatic triglyceride levels.
source: In addition, components of the extracellular matrix were enriched (2.91 fold, adjusted p = 5.89 × 10−3) and were also predominantly (13 out of 17 genes) higher in steatotic livers (Table 3).
evidence: The results section reports pathway enrichment analysis results.

claim: Complement and the coagulation cascade were specifically enriched (3.03 fold, adjusted p = 3.93 × 10−3) among the top 1000 hepatic genes correlated with hepatic triglyceride levels.
source: Complement and the coagulation cascade were specifically enriched (3.03 fold, adjusted p = 3.93 × 10−3) and the genes were predominantly (15 out of 18 genes) lower in steatotic livers.
evidence: The results section reports pathway enrichment analysis results.

claim: In the adipose tissue, mitotic cell cycle, actin polymerization, cytoskeleton organization, immune response, response to wounding, leukocyte activation and positive regulation of cytokine production, lysosome pathway, and B cell receptor signaling were all enriched among the top 1000 genes correlated with hepatic triglyceride levels.
source: In the adipose tissue, mitotic cell cycle, actin polymerization, cytoskeleton organization, immune response, response to wounding, leukocyte activation and positive regulation of cytokine production, lysosome pathway, and B cell receptor signaling were all enriched (Table 4).
evidence: The results section reports pathway enrichment analysis results for adipose tissue.

claim: Inflammation in adipose tissue likely plays a role in the development of NAFLD.
source: These findings suggest that inflammation in adipose tissue likely plays a role in the development of NAFLD.
evidence: The results section interprets the pathway enrichment findings.

claim: One genome-wide significant peak associated with hepatic triglyceride content was identified on chromosome 7.
source: We identified one genome-wide significant peak associated with hepatic TG content on chromosome 7 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section reports GWAS findings, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The chromosome 7 peak does not overlap with any loci identified for obesity and insulin resistance in the same cohort of mice.
source: This peak does not overlap with any loci identified for obesity and insulin resistance in the same cohort of mice (Parks et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: The results section compares the chromosome 7 locus to previously identified loci.

claim: The peak locus on chromosome 7 still reached genome-wide significance when association mapping was conditioned using adiposity or insulin resistance as covariates.
source: In addition, the peak locus on chromosome 7 still reached genome-wide significance when association mapping was conditioned using adiposity (% fat) or insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) as covariates (Figure 6), indicating that the effect of the chromosome 7 locus on hepatic steatosis is independent of obesity and diabetes.
evidence: The results section reports conditional GWAS results, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: The peak SNP (rs32519715, p = 1.15 × 10−6) on chromosome 7 falls in a linkage disequilibrium block containing 17 genes.
source: The peak SNP (rs32519715, p = 1.15 × 10−6) falls in a LD block containing 17 genes (Figure 5B and Table 6).
evidence: The results section reports the peak SNP and candidate genes, with reference to Figure 5B and Table 6.

claim: Three suggestive peaks on chromosomes 3, 9, and 11 passed the genome-wide significant threshold of 5% FDR.
source: Three suggestive peaks, on chromosomes 3 (rs3708683; p = 5.47 × 10−5), 9 (rs36804270; p = 1.30 × 10−5), and 11 (rs13481015; p = 1.72 × 10−5) passed the genome-wide significant threshold of 5% FDR (p = 1.34 × 10−4).
evidence: The results section reports additional suggestive GWAS peaks.

claim: Among the candidate genes in the chromosome 7 locus, only three genes (Coq7, Gde1, and Knop1) have significant cis-eQTL and are also expressed in the liver.
source: Among the candidate genes in the chromosome 7 locus, only three genes (Coq7, Gde1, and Knop1) have significant cis-eQTL and are also expressed in the liver (Tables 6, 8).
evidence: The results section reports cis-eQTL analysis results.

claim: Hepatic triglyceride levels correlated with Gde1 expression in both the liver (r = 0.35, p = 1.5 × 10−4) and adipose tissue (r = −0.21, p = 1.6 × 10−3).
source: Hepatic TG levels correlated with Gde1 expression in both the liver (r = 0.35, p = 1.5 × 10−4) and adipose tissue (r = −0.21, p = 1.6 × 10−3) (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between Gde1 expression and hepatic TG, with reference to figures.

claim: Knop1 expression correlated with hepatic triglyceride levels in the liver (r = 0.29, p = 2.5 × 10−2) but not in the adipose tissue (r = 0.14, p = 0.133).
source: Likewise, Knop1 expression correlated with hepatic TG levels (r = 0.29, p = 2.5 × 10−2, Figure 7B) but not in the adipose tissue (r = 0.14, p = 0.133).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between Knop1 expression and hepatic TG, with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Hepatic triglyceride levels did not correlate with Coq7 expression in the liver (r = 0.09, p = 0.368) or adipose tissue (r = −0.14, p = 0.142).
source: On the other hand, hepatic TG levels did not correlate with Coq7 expression in the liver (r = 0.09, p = 0.368) or adipose tissue (r = −0.14, p = 0.142).
evidence: The results section reports the lack of correlation between Coq7 expression and hepatic TG.

claim: Gde1 encodes glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase 1, a ubiquitously expressed enzyme involved in phospholipid metabolism.
source: Gde1 (also known as MIR16) encodes glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase 1, a ubiquitously expressed enzyme involved in phospholipid metabolism, whereas Knop1 encodes a lysine-rich nucleolar protein.
evidence: The results section describes the function of Gde1.

claim: Knop1 encodes a lysine-rich nucleolar protein.
source: Gde1 (also known as MIR16) encodes glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase 1, a ubiquitously expressed enzyme involved in phospholipid metabolism, whereas Knop1 encodes a lysine-rich nucleolar protein.
evidence: The results section describes the function of Knop1.

claim: Neither Gde1 nor Knop1 has previously been identified in studies related to triglyceride or lipid metabolism.
source: Neither of these two genes has previously been identified in studies related to TG or lipid metabolism.
evidence: The results section states the novelty of these candidate genes.

claim: The Q117R substitution in Syt7 was predicted to be deleterious.
source: Only the Q117R substitution in Syt7 was predicted to be deleterious.
evidence: The results section reports the predicted effect of a missense variant in Syt7.

claim: Ablation of Syt7 has been shown to decrease insulin and glucagon secretion in pancreatic cells.
source: Ablation of Syt7 has been shown to decrease insulin and glucagon secretion in pancreatic cells (Gustavsson et al., 2008, 2009).
evidence: The results section cites literature on Syt7 function.

claim: The weight of livers from Gde1-overexpressing mice was 40% higher than that of the control.
source: While there was no significant difference in body weight, the weight of livers from Gde1-overexpressing mice was 40% higher than that of the control (Figure 8B, p = 4.7 × 10−5).
evidence: The results section reports the effect of Gde1 overexpression on liver weight, with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: Plasma triglyceride, total cholesterol, and free fatty acids were all elevated in Ad-Gde1 mice.
source: In addition, plasma TG, TC, and FFA were all elevated in Ad-Gde1 mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: The results section reports the effect of Gde1 overexpression on plasma lipids, with reference to Figure 8C.

claim: Livers from Gde1-overexpressing mice contained significantly higher fat content (p = 0.0002).
source: MRI analysis showed that livers from Gde1-overexpressing mice contained significantly higher fat content (Figure 8D, p = 0.0002).
evidence: The results section reports MRI analysis results, with reference to Figure 8D.

claim: The increase in hepatic fat content in Gde1-overexpressing mice was primarily due to increased accumulation of triglyceride (p = 0.014).
source: Lipid analyses revealed that the increase in hepatic fat content was primarily due to increased accumulation of TG (Figure 8E, p = 0.014), as hepatic TC and phospholipid content were not significantly different from the control group (Figure 8F,G).
evidence: The results section reports lipid analysis results, with reference to figures.

claim: Hepatic genes involved in triglyceride biosynthesis (Fasn, Dgat2, and Gpd1) were down-regulated in mice overexpressing Gde1.
source: Hepatic genes involved in TG biosynthesis (Fasn, Dgat2, and Gpd1) were down-regulated in mice overexpressing Gde1 (Figure 8H).
evidence: The results section reports gene expression changes in Gde1-overexpressing mice, with reference to Figure 8H.

claim: Knockdown of Gde1 led to a significant decrease in hepatic triglyceride content (p = 0.011).
source: In contrast to the overexpression studies, knockdown of Gde1 led to a significant decrease in hepatic TG content (Figure 9C, p = 0.011), whereas TC and phospholipid levels were not different from the control group (Figure 9D,E).
evidence: The results section reports the effect of Gde1 knockdown on hepatic TG, with reference to Figure 9C.

claim: Expression of lipogenic genes (Fasn, Dgat2, and Gpd1) was increased in Gde1-knockdown livers.
source: Similarly, expression of lipogenic genes (Fasn, Dgat2, and Gpd1) was increased in Gde1-knockdown livers (Figure 9F).
evidence: The results section reports gene expression changes in Gde1-knockdown mice, with reference to Figure 9F.

claim: The overexpression and knockdown studies support a causal role for Gde1 in hepatic steatosis under the chromosome 7 locus.
source: These findings support a causal role for Gde1 in hepatic steatosis under the chromosome 7 locus.
evidence: The results section interprets the functional validation experiments.

claim: The direction of the effect of Gde1 expression with respect to hepatic triglyceride levels in the overexpression and knockdown studies is consistent with that observed in the HMDP in liver.
source: It is noteworthy that the direction of the effect of Gde1 expression with respect to hepatic TG levels in these studies is consistent with that observed in the HMDP in liver (i.e., a positive correlation).
evidence: The results section notes the consistency between functional validation and HMDP observations.

claim: Correlation analysis revealed a significant negative relationship between hepatic triglyceride levels and plasma levels of arginine (r = −0.53, p = 9.85 × 10−12).
source: Correlation analysis revealed a significant negative relationship between hepatic TG levels and plasma levels of arginine (r = −0.53, p = 9.85 × 10−12) and its degradative metabolite ornithine (r = −0.18, p = 0.027) (Figure 10A,B), whereas citrulline, another degradative metabolite of arginine, showed a positive correlation with hepatic TG content (r = 0.18, p = 0.034, Figure 10C).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between plasma metabolites and hepatic TG, with reference to figures.

claim: Plasma levels of ornithine showed a negative correlation with hepatic triglyceride levels (r = −0.18, p = 0.027).
source: Correlation analysis revealed a significant negative relationship between hepatic TG levels and plasma levels of arginine (r = −0.53, p = 9.85 × 10−12) and its degradative metabolite ornithine (r = −0.18, p = 0.027) (Figure 10A,B), whereas citrulline, another degradative metabolite of arginine, showed a positive correlation with hepatic TG content (r = 0.18, p = 0.034, Figure 10C).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between plasma metabolites and hepatic TG, with reference to figures.

claim: Citrulline showed a positive correlation with hepatic triglyceride content (r = 0.18, p = 0.034).
source: Correlation analysis revealed a significant negative relationship between hepatic TG levels and plasma levels of arginine (r = −0.53, p = 9.85 × 10−12) and its degradative metabolite ornithine (r = −0.18, p = 0.027) (Figure 10A,B), whereas citrulline, another degradative metabolite of arginine, showed a positive correlation with hepatic TG content (r = 0.18, p = 0.034, Figure 10C).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between plasma metabolites and hepatic TG, with reference to figures.

claim: Hepatic triglyceride levels were positively correlated with plasma levels of trimethylamine-N-oxide (r = 0.18, p = 0.034).
source: Hepatic TG levels were positively correlated with plasma levels of trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMANO, r = 0.18, p = 0.034, Figure 10D).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between TMANO and hepatic TG, with reference to Figure 10D.

claim: Increased TMANO levels have previously been implicated in the susceptibility of strain 129S6 mice to diet-induced impaired glucose homeostasis and NAFLD.
source: Increased TMANO levels have previously been implicated in the susceptibility of strain 129S6 mice to diet-induced impaired glucose homeostasis and NAFLD (Dumas et al., 2006).
evidence: The results section cites literature on TMANO in NAFLD.

claim: TMANO levels are strongly associated with atherosclerosis.
source: TMANO levels are regulated by both genetic and dietary factors and are strongly associated with atherosclerosis (Bennett et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section cites literature on TMANO and atherosclerosis.

claim: FMO5 expression exhibited a significant correlation with hepatic triglyceride content (r = 0.46, p = 2.71 × 10−7).
source: No significant correlation between FMO3 expression and hepatic TG content was observed; however, among the 5 members in the FMO family, FMO5 expression exhibited a significant correlation with hepatic TG content (r = 0.46, p = 2.71 × 10−7).
evidence: The results section reports a correlation between FMO5 expression and hepatic TG.

claim: Hepatic triglyceride content was positively associated with plasma creatine (r = 0.23, p = 6 × 10−3) and creatinine levels (r = 0.25, p = 6 × 10−3).
source: Hepatic TG content was also positively associated with plasma creatine (r = 0.23, p = 6 × 10−3, Figure 10E) and creatinine levels (r = 0.25, p = 6 × 10−3, Figure 10F).
evidence: The results section reports correlations between creatine/creatinine and hepatic TG, with reference to figures.

claim: There was no significant correlation between hepatic triglyceride levels and overall microbial diversity, as determined by Shannon diversity index.
source: There was no significant correlation between hepatic TG levels and overall microbial diversity, as determined by Shannon diversity index (Mills and& Wassel, 1980).
evidence: The results section reports the lack of correlation between hepatic TG and microbial diversity.

claim: For the bacterial families and genera detected at significant levels, none were significantly associated with hepatic triglyceride levels at 5% FDR.
source: For the bacterial families and genera detected at significant levels, none were significantly associated with hepatic TG levels (5% FDR) (Table 10).
evidence: The results section reports the lack of significant associations between microbiota and hepatic TG.

claim: Coprococcus and Oscillospira were positively associated with hepatic unesterified cholesterol levels.
source: Coprococcus and Oscillospira were positively associated with hepatic unesterified cholesterol levels, whereas negative associations were observed with Blatuia.
evidence: The results section reports associations between microbiota and hepatic cholesterol.

claim: Blautia was negatively associated with hepatic unesterified cholesterol levels.
source: Coprococcus and Oscillospira were positively associated with hepatic unesterified cholesterol levels, whereas negative associations were observed with Blatuia.
evidence: The results section reports associations between microbiota and hepatic cholesterol.

claim: Blautia and Allobaculum were negatively associated with hepatic total cholesterol.
source: Blautia and Allobaculum were negatively associated with TC.
evidence: The results section reports associations between microbiota and hepatic total cholesterol.

claim: Coprococcus and Oscillospira were positively associated with hepatic phospholipids.
source: Coprococcus and Oscillospira were positively associated with phospholipids, whereas Ruminococcus showed negative association (Table 10).
evidence: The results section reports associations between microbiota and hepatic phospholipids.

claim: Ruminococcus showed negative association with hepatic phospholipids.
source: Coprococcus and Oscillospira were positively associated with phospholipids, whereas Ruminococcus showed negative association (Table 10).
evidence: The results section reports associations between microbiota and hepatic phospholipids.

claim: Gde1 catalyzes the degradation of glycerophosphoethanolamine and glycerophosphocholine.
source: Gde1 encodes glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase 1 (EC 3.1.4.46), a broadly expressed integral membrane glycoprotein, which catalyzes the degradation of glycerophosphoethanolamine and glycerophosphocholine (Okazaki et al., 2010; Simon and& Cravatt, 2010).
evidence: The discussion describes the enzymatic function of Gde1.

claim: Two forms of the GDE1 protein (approximately 37 kDa and 43 kDa) were detected in Western blots, which is likely due to variable glycosylation.
source: Two forms of the protein (∼37 kDa and 43 kDa) were detected in Western blots of endogenous and adenoviral overexpressed GDE1, which is likely be due to variable glycosylation as previously documented (Zheng et al., 2000).
evidence: The discussion explains the observed protein forms of GDE1.

claim: Increased expression of Cd36 in Gde1-overexpressing livers raises the possibility that Cd36 acts as a mediator of the effect of Gde1 through its lipid transport activity.
source: Increased expression of Cd36 in Gde1-overexpressing livers raises the possibility that Cd36 acts as a mediator of the effect of Gde1 through its lipid transport activity.
evidence: The discussion presents a hypothesis about the mechanism of Gde1 action.

claim: One of the products of the Gde1 enzymatic reaction is glycerol-3-phosphate.
source: One of the products of the Gde1 enzymatic reaction is glycerol-3-phosphate, which can be converted to phosphatidate by glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) and subsequently dephosphorylated by the phosphatidate phosphatase lipin to form diacylglycerol (DAG).
evidence: The discussion describes the biochemical pathway involving Gde1 products.

claim: Glycerol-3-phosphate can be converted to phosphatidate by glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase.
source: One of the products of the Gde1 enzymatic reaction is glycerol-3-phosphate, which can be converted to phosphatidate by glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) and subsequently dephosphorylated by the phosphatidate phosphatase lipin to form diacylglycerol (DAG).
evidence: The discussion describes the biochemical pathway involving glycerol-3-phosphate.

claim: Phosphatidate can be dephosphorylated by the phosphatidate phosphatase lipin to form diacylglycerol.
source: One of the products of the Gde1 enzymatic reaction is glycerol-3-phosphate, which can be converted to phosphatidate by glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) and subsequently dephosphorylated by the phosphatidate phosphatase lipin to form diacylglycerol (DAG).
evidence: The discussion describes the biochemical pathway involving phosphatidate.

claim: Diacylglycerol can be acylated by DGAT to form triglyceride.
source: DAG can then be acylated by DGAT to form TG.
evidence: The discussion describes the final step of TG synthesis.

claim: The negative correlation of adipose Gde1 expression and hepatic triglyceride may be due to a different role of glycerol-3-phosphate in the adipose tissue.
source: The negative correlation of adipose Gde1 expression and hepatic TG may be due to a different role of glycerol-3-phosphate in the adipose tissue.
evidence: The discussion presents a hypothesis about tissue-specific effects of Gde1.

claim: Increased glycerol-3-phosphate production in the adipose tissue would promote fatty acid re-esterification, leading to a decrease in fatty acid release to the circulation.
source: Increased glycerol-3-phosphate production (when Gde1 expression is high) in the adipose tissue would promote FA re-esterification, leading to a decrease in FA release to the circulation.
evidence: The discussion presents a hypothesis about the mechanism of Gde1 in adipose tissue.

claim: The opposite pattern of regulation of Gde1 in liver and adipose implicates tissue-specific regulatory elements.
source: The opposite pattern of regulation of Gde1 implicates tissue-specific regulatory elements.
evidence: The discussion interprets the differential regulation of Gde1.

claim: Mouse ENCODE data showed that there are differences in DNA hypersensitive sites in the Gde1 gene region, suggesting differences in DNA accessibility and transcription factor binding in the liver and adipose tissue.
source: Mouse ENCODE data (Yue et al., 2014) showed that there are differences in DNA hypersensitive sites in the gene region, suggesting that there may be differences in DNA accessibility and transcription factor binding in the liver and adipose tissue.
evidence: The discussion cites ENCODE data to support tissue-specific regulation.

claim: The enrichment of mitochondrial genes in steatotic livers suggests that disrupted mitochondrial bioenergetics may play a role in NAFLD pathobiology.
source: Our observed enrichment of mitochondrial genes in steatotic livers suggests that disrupted mitochondrial bioenergetics may play a role in NAFLD pathobiology.
evidence: The discussion interprets the pathway enrichment findings.

claim: Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet induced NAFLD with reduced mitochondrial oxidation and increased ROS production.
source: This is in accordance with finding that chronic consumption of a HF diet-induced NAFLD with reduced mitochondrial oxidation and increased ROS production (Mantena et al., 2009).
evidence: The discussion cites literature on mitochondrial function in NAFLD.

claim: Obesity-induced steatosis has been linked to decreased hepatic ATP synthesis.
source: Obesity-induced steatosis has also been linked to decreased hepatic ATP synthesis (Chavin et al., 1999).
evidence: The discussion cites literature on ATP synthesis in steatosis.

claim: The inverse relationship between arginine levels and hepatic triglyceride content may be due to increased arginine degradation in steatotic mice.
source: The inverse relationship between arginine levels and hepatic TG content may be due to increased arginine degradation in steatotic mice.
evidence: The discussion presents a hypothesis about arginine metabolism.

claim: An arginine-deficient diet induced hepatic steatosis in rats.
source: Previous studies have shown that an arginine-deficient diet-induced hepatic steatosis in rats (Milner and& Hassan, 1981).
evidence: The discussion cites literature on arginine deficiency and steatosis.

claim: The levels of arginase 1 were increased in steatotic livers from mice fed a high-fat diet.
source: The levels of arginase 1, which catabolizes L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine, were increased in steatotic livers from mice fed a high-fat diet (Eccleston et al., 2011).
evidence: The discussion cites literature on arginase 1 in steatotic livers.

claim: Low levels of arginine may lead to increased gut bacterial and endotoxin translocation, which promotes liver inflammation and NAFLD progression.
source: Low levels of arginine may lead to increased gut bacterial and endotoxin translocation, which promotes liver inflammation and NAFLD progression.
evidence: The discussion presents a hypothesis about the role of arginine in NAFLD.

claim: Studies in humans showed a large reduction in abundance of Coprococcus and Oscillospira in obese and NASH subjects.
source: Studies in humans showed a large reduction in abundance of these microbes in obese and NASH subjects (Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion cites literature on microbiota in human obesity and NASH.

claim: Studies of diet-induced obesity in mice suggest that abundance of Oscillospira may affect gut barrier function in the proximal colon.
source: Studies of diet-induced obesity in mice suggest that abundance of Oscillospira may affect gut barrier function in the proximal colon (Lam et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion cites literature on Oscillospira and gut barrier function.
